detail.abstract:
For nearly a century and a half, the Supreme Court of Ohio has declared, without defining, the governing principle of littoral property law along Lake Erie: the boundary between the state’s public trust in the waters and the private upland title of the littoral owner is the “natural shoreline” — the line at which the water usually stands when free from disturbing causes. Sloan v. Biemiller (1878) borrowed the phrase from Illinois; Merrill v. Ohio Department of Natural Resources (2011) reaffirmed it unanimously. Neither case, nor any case in the 148 years between them, has ever defined what a disturbing cause is. No legislature has supplied the definition. No regulatory body has operationalized it. And until now, no legal scholar has attempted to do so.

This article fills that gap. The stakes are not academic. Approximately 15,500 littoral landowners along Ohio’s 311-mile Lake Erie coastline hold title that terminates, by law, at a boundary no one can reliably locate. Littoral owners seek certainty and the full exercise of their constitutionally protected property rights to a defined, ascertainable line. Environmental organizations and recreational users press an equal but opposite interest: the assurance that the public trust in the waters of Lake Erie is never severed from the water’s edge by an artificially frozen boundary. Both interests are legitimate. Both are currently unserved.

This article argues that the answer has been embedded in the ancient common law for centuries, requiring only that it be recognized and applied. The common law of littoral property has long distinguished two categories of forces that alter the water’s edge. The first category — accretion, reliction, erosion, and submersion — consists of processes that are gradual, long-term, imperceptible while underway, and ordinary in character. These processes have always been recognized as title-changers: they move the boundary with the water. The second category — avulsion, storm surge, seiche, atmospheric pressure change, ice effects, wind tide, and similar sudden forces — consists of processes that are abrupt, short-term, dramatic, and perceptible while underway. These are the disturbing causes: they do not move the boundary, because the water’s position under their influence is not the water’s natural position.

The key is perceptibility at the time the process is underway, not measurability after the fact. A disturbing cause can be seen happening. Accretion, reliction, erosion, and submersion cannot be perceived while they occur, only measured in retrospect. That distinction — ancient, principled, already embedded in American property law and confirmed by the Supreme Court of the United States — resolves the definitional problem that Merrill left open. The natural shoreline is the water’s edge in its ordinary, undisturbed condition: mobile across time with the gradual forces the common law has always recognized as title-changers, but stable against the perceptible disturbances the common law has never permitted to alter property boundaries.

title: A Role for Artificial Intelligence in a Politicized Immigration World
affiliations: Drexel University Thomas R. Kline School of Law

detail.title: A Role for Artificial Intelligence in a Politicized Immigration World
detail.abstract:
Many debates about artificial intelligence boil down to one central question: who is better (or worse) at making decisions? Artificial intelligence doomsayers worry that AI will supplant human decision-making, with catastrophic consequences that render humans expendable. On the other hand, if AI can overcome human bias and nefarious intent, it holds the possibility of shielding humanity from its worst impulses.

This tension is evident in the realm of immigration policy, which for the last 100 years has revealed the frailties of human decision-making. Immigration debates prompt racial and ethnic stereotyping, reactionary proposals, and deliberate refusals to examine evidence or prioritize fact-based decisions. Introducing AI tools can add fuel to the fire. It can promote mass surveillance of noncitizens, mining social medial to find reasons to revoke visas, and perpetuate racial and ethnic bias.

While staying clear eyed about these risk, this essay suggests that immigration policymaking displays how human decision-making is so flawed that enabling greater use of AI technology--with appropriate guardrails and guiding principles--may actually help protect us from ourselves. It is possible that AI tools, which lack motivation and intent, can provide a buffer against human cruelty, implicit bias, and capacity limitations. This essay offers three principles to guide AI with respect to immigration. First, AI technology can offer independence and protection from political interference over day-to-day agency decisions. Second, given the way the current presidential administration is dismantling the federal workforce, AI tools may prove necessary for processing immigration applications and reducing backlogs. Third, AI use should be guided by the principle of affirming human dignity. In that way, AI can address situations where a noncitizen seeks the government's help while simultaneously protecting against the government's non-consensual intrusion upon individual rights, such as through expanded surveillance.

title: Integration of Vastu Principles in Sugarcane Disease Management: A Comparative Agro-Spatial Study on Red Rot and Major Diseases in Sugarcane Cultivation

detail.title: Integration of Vastu Principles in Sugarcane Disease Management: A Comparative Agro-Spatial Study on Red Rot and Major Diseases in Sugarcane Cultivation
detail.abstract: Sugarcane cultivation remains vulnerable to several destructive diseases, including Red Rot, Smut, Wilt, and Grassy Shoot Disease. Conventional agricultural science associates these diseases with fungal pathogens, climatic conditions, water stagnation, monocropping, poor drainage, and infected planting material. However, traditional Indian environmental sciences such as Vastu Shastra propose that land orientation, directional balance, solar movement, airflow patterns, geomagnetic alignment, and water placement may also influence ecological harmony and biological health. This research paper investigates the relationship between agricultural spatial organisation and disease development in sugarcane cultivation through an interdisciplinary framework integrating plant pathology, environmental science, sustainable agriculture, and Vastu-based land planning. The study particularly focuses on the influence of moisture retention, sunlight exposure, field slope, air circulation, and irrigation layout on the prevalence of fungal diseases such as Red Rot. A comparative conceptual analysis has been conducted using climatic observations from tropical sugarcane-producing regions including Tamil Nadu (India) and Peru. The study proposes that certain traditional Vastu principles may correspond with scientifically measurable environmental variables including humidity management, ultraviolet exposure, drainage efficiency, and microclimatic regulation. The paper does not claim supernatural causation; rather, it explores whether traditional spatial agricultural knowledge may contribute toward healthier agro-ecological systems and sustainable disease management. The study recommends future experimental field trials for scientific validation of agro-spatial farming models.

title: The Institutional Origins of AI: Evidence from Large Language Models
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Institutional Origins of AI: Evidence from Large Language Models
detail.abstract: Organizations adopt artificial intelligence on cost and capability. They do not ask what else travels with the efficiency. This paper argues that institutional logics are embedded in AI systems through the production process itself-carried into every organization that adopts them, whether recognized or not. We develop a production-position framework identifying eight dimensions along which AI producers vary: organizational type, regulatory context, training data, human feedback labor, evaluation regimes, market positioning, funding structure, and distillation lineage. Drawing on institutional carrier theory (Scott, 2003) and epistemic cultures (Knorr-Cetina, 1999), we theorize AI as a new class of institutional carrier-one that transports institutional dispositions without the communities of practice that produced them. Two empirical studies test this framework. Study 1 administers 25 organizational decision scenarios to five frontier models from four institutional origins (3,125 observations): models diverge systematically on 68% of scenarios while maintaining 91.4% within-model consistency. Study 2 administers six open-ended knowledge-production tasks to nine frontier models from four institutional contexts (162 outputs): institutional signatures are detectable at the embedding level but not at the surface, manifesting as divergent epistemic commitments about what constitutes evidence, explanation, and legitimate inquiry. When knowledge workers collaborate with different AI, they encounter different epistemic cultures-not because of capability differences but because of production-origin differences. The configuration of production dimensions predicts behavioral similarity better than any single dimension-including geographic origin. AI selection is institutional selection. "Does it work?" must be joined by "whose world travels with it?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare No potential conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: In humanitarian logistics (HL), prioritizing of relief item distribution under limited transportation capacity is an important and practical problem that relief organizations face. The priority not only depends on the dynamic demand urgency, but also on the different equity concerns between distribution center (DC) managers and point of distribution (POD) managers. In this paper, through field investigations, we adopt deprivation cost to capture the dynamic priority among different relief items like drinking water or tents, and envy to represent the equity perceptions of victims, based on which we study a distribution-allocation problem to answer the following research questions: (1) Which kind of relief item at which time point should be distributed in priority with limited transportation capacity? (2) What’s the impact on distribution strategy when there are misalignments between DC and POD managers? Should the DC managers take envy of victims into account? We build a bi-objective model which minimizes the sum of deprivation cost of different relief items and the possible penalty caused by envy. A case study is conducted based on the real-world data of Lushan earthquake. The result proves the feasibility of using deprivation cost functions to demonstrate relief item priority dynamics in distribution-allocation problems, and shows that the consideration of envy may greatly influence the optimal distribution strategy and change the priority of relief items. Summarizing, this paper presents an original approach to incorporate the dynamic priority of relief item distribution with consideration of divergent equity concerns.

detail.title: Integrated Human-Robot Safety Management System (I-HR-SMS): A Validated Measurement Framework for Worker Safety Perception in Collaborative Robot Environments

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
The rapid expansion of collaborative robots (cobots) in industrial environments has introduced new, insufficiently understood safety challenges at the point of human‑robot interaction (HRI). This study presents the Integrated Human‑Robot Safety Management System (I‑HR‑SMS), a three‑pillar measurement framework—Hazard Recognition and Signal Detection, Procedural Adherence and Safety Compliance, and Adaptive Response and Recovery—designed to quantify worker safety perceptions during discrete HRI events. Unlike prior research that treats the worker or organization as the unit of analysis, the I‑HR‑SMS designates the HRI event as the analytic unit, enabling detection of within‑person and cross‑sector variability across three deployment environments: Humanoid Robotics, Airport Luggage Operations, and Warehousing and Manufacturing.

A 36‑item, 6th‑grade‑literacy‑calibrated digital survey instrument was developed and administered using a gamified delivery platform to maximize comprehension and response completeness. A five‑stage multistage cluster sampling strategy (3 sectors × 5 industries × 5 cities × 3 shifts) produced a theoretical frame of 225 shift‑level sampling units, from which systematically sampled HRI events yielded a target sample of N = 102 event‑level records, consistent with G*Power requirements for medium‑effect multiple regression. The instrument includes three validated composite scales aligned to the I‑HR‑SMS pillars and incorporates attention‑check items to ensure data integrity.

The I‑HR‑SMS framework advances HRI safety research by (1) operationalizing safety perception at the event level, (2) integrating literacy‑aligned item design for frontline industrial workers, and (3) enabling comparative analysis across heterogeneous cobot deployment contexts. Findings are positioned to inform both theoretical models of safety climate and practical safety management strategies aligned with NIOSH priorities and A3 Robotics collaborative safety standards.

detail.abstract: Healthcare organizations manage operational tasks such as appointment scheduling, wellness reminders, transportation coordination, and patient follow-ups. The majority of conversational healthcare systems now in use rely on third-party services and centralized cloud-based transformer models [1], [2], which raises issues with patient privacy, operating costs, regulatory compliance, and reliance on outside infrastructure. Furthermore, asynchronous communication and dependable workflow recovery following disruptions are not adequately supported by many chatbot systems, which are designed for real-time engagement [5]-[8]. This work offers a lightweight, privacy-preserving asynchronous conversational framework for automated healthcare appointment scheduling using deterministic workflow execution and persistent-state recovery. The suggested design, in contrast to traditional cloud-hosted chatbot systems, uses recovery-driven queue processing and SQL-based persistent-state monitoring to preserve multi-stage scheduling continuity in the event of interrupted and delayed communication. The system operates entirely on-premises using standard SMTP and IMAP protocols and was implemented in Python with Microsoft SQL Server, with deployment as a standalone executable using PyInstaller [9], [10]. Experimental evaluation using 106 synthetic patient records generated with the Synthea platform [11] produced 283 asynchronous conversational workflow events. Controlled fault-injection testing demonstrated successful persistent-state recovery after simulated crashes, zero duplicate scheduling events, zero message loss, and reliable workflow continuity. The proposed architecture provides a cost-effective, HIPAA-oriented, privacy-preserving alternative for smaller healthcare organizations requiring dependable appointment scheduling without centralized cloud infrastructure.

detail.abstract: Background: Cancer epidemiologists increasingly contribute evidence evaluating the causal effect of policies on cancer outcomes. The validity of such evidence relies on attention to conceptual, analytic, and data aspects of causal inference research. To highlight these important aspects and contribute our own policy-relevant evidence, we aimed to evaluate Virginia's Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination mandate on cervical cancer incidence. HPV vaccination mandates were intended to increase vaccine uptake and reduce cervical cancer incidence, yet causal evidence on cancer incidence remains scarce. Virginia implemented an HPV vaccine mandate in 2008, providing an opportunity to leverage this natural experiment within a causal inference framework. Methods: After motivating why traditional methods may be invalid, we estimated the effect of Virginia's HPV vaccine mandate on cervical cancer incidence among females aged 20-24 with a synthetic control triple differences design. Our post-period begins in 2016, when the first mandate-exposed cohort reached ages 20-24. State-level cancer registry data (2003-2019) were used to compare Virginia's incidence trends to a weighted combination of control states, while adjusting for within-state trends across age groups exposed and not exposed to the mandate. Results: Cervical cancer incidence among 20-24-year-old females declined over time in both Virginia and comparison states. Ignoring within-state differential age-group trends, the synthetic control difference-indifferences design showed no evidence of any effect. The synthetic control triple difference design estimated that Virginia's mandate was associated with 1.6 additional cervical cancer cases per 100,000 population (CI = 0.4, 2.7). Alternative specifications, including adjustments for screening and multiple sensitivity analyses, produced consistent results in direction and inference.

title: From Rainy Day Funds to Digital Gold: The Politics and Prudence of State-Level Bitcoin Reserves

detail.title: From Rainy Day Funds to Digital Gold: The Politics and Prudence of State-Level Bitcoin Reserves
detail.abstract: Beginning in 2025, a growing number of U.S. states enacted legislation authorizing public funds to be invested in Bitcoin and other digital assets, marking a significant departure from traditional public finance principles that prioritize liquidity, stability, and capital preservation. This paper examines the national trend of statelevel cryptocurrency reserve legislation, with a detailed case study of Texas, the first state to fund such a reserve. The analysis synthesizes legislative frameworks, investment mechanics, political motivations, and documented outcomes through May 2026. Particular attenion is paid to fiscal prudence concerns raised by economists and lawmakers, including volatility risk, taxpayer exposure, and governance challenges. While proponents argue these initiatives hedge against inflation and signal economic competitiveness, the evidence to date suggests substantial risks have materialized, with Texas's initial purchase showing an unrealized loss exceeding 11%. The paper concludes that current initiatives remain more politically symbolic than financially substantive, though their long-term implications for public finance warrant continued scrutiny.

detail.abstract: In this research we uncover a tidy=sustainable association, which informs consumers’ evaluations and decisions. Across ten studies (N=2700), we find that consumers judge tidy (versus untidy) places, as well as objects within those places, to be more sustainable. We posit that consumers develop this learnt association because of the link through the multi-faceted concept of minimalism, which encompasses aspects related to aesthetics (as represented in spatial tidiness) and consumption (with impact sustainability outcomes). Supporting this mechanism, we show that spatial tidiness increases perceptions of minimalistic consumption practices—where consumers perceive tidy spaces as reflecting reduced number of possessions and mindful consumption—which in turn increases sustainability evaluations. Importantly, we show that the tidy=sustainable association operates bidirectionally, is amplified among consumers with higher minimalism values, and has downstream consequences on purchase, recommendation, and joint consumption decisions.

detail.abstract: Complex infrastructure projects fail at integration. The failure is structural before it is cultural: it stems from decisions about organisational design, contractual form, and the allocation of interface risk, made years before any construction begins. This paper develops an analytical framework to explain why integration fails on complex infrastructure projects and what a viable alternative looks like. Drawing on three UK cases (Crossrail (the Elizabeth line), the A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon road improvement, and the Thames Tideway Tunnel), the paper argues that the dominant project delivery model concentrates integration risk within a single client body without establishing the structural mechanisms that such concentration requires. The conventional response, a central authority board, only relocates the problem it is meant to solve. The alternative, demonstrated at Tideway and partially prefigured at the A14, is organisational design that embeds lateral connections between contractors in governance structures, encodes them in commercial terms, and pushes decision authority to where knowledge sits. The paper identifies three principles: integration is a structural problem, not a cultural one; empowerment requires verified competence and aligned incentives; and lateral connections must be designed in, not improvised. Implications are drawn for contract design, project leadership diagnostics, and the ongoing reform of the NEC contract suite.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has emerged as one of the most transformative technological forces in human history. The speed and scale of AI adoption are unprecedented-ChatGPT reached 100 million users in two months, and by 2026 over 400 million users generate 15 billion queries weekly. However, this rapid integration raises urgent questions about hidden costs to human cognition, skills, and society. This paper provides a comprehensive, evidence-based examination of AI's promises and perils. It synthesizes findings from recent empirical studies including the Microsoft 2025 Critical Thinking survey (n=319 knowledge workers), the Springer 2025 scoping review on AI addiction (27.8% prevalence), the Duke 2025 creativity study (47% higher homogeneity in AI output), the Yurt and Kuşci 2025 study (n=422, β =-0.37, p<.001 for AI use on critical thinking), the Save My Exams 2026 survey (93% of students using AI), and the NBER 2026 economic forecasting study (10 million potential job losses under rapid AI scenarios). The paper introduces the concept of Cognitive Dependency Syndrome, examines AI's impact across employment, education, mental health, geopolitics, and existential risk, and proposes a five-level AI Use Maturity Model as a practical framework for balanced integration. The central argument is that AI's long-term impact will be determined by the intentionality with which societies approach regulation, education, and the preservation of essential human skills.

title: Response Adaptivity Across Clinical Trials in Portfolios of Biomedical Innovations

detail.title: Response Adaptivity Across Clinical Trials in Portfolios of Biomedical Innovations
detail.abstract: New medical treatments are costly to develop and unlikely to successfully make their way through clinical trials, market access, and reimbursement. Moreover, new treatments for rare diseases are limited in both patient populations and reimbursement levels, further reducing their attractiveness as an investment. To increase the incentive to develop new treatments, portfolios of investments in new treatments in clinical trials have been proposed to financially de-risk drug development. We explore an important lever for further improving the incentives to develop treatments that is new in the context of biomedical portfolios: response-adaptive pilot studies in clinical trials that allow investments to be adjusted across projects as data are observed and that account for the importance of cost-effectiveness in gaining market access. We propose and analyze a model that shows that even a modest level of response adaptivity can materially improve financial outcomes from portfolios and improve the chances of new treatments making it to market, particularly when investment amounts are limited. We derive expected value of information heuristics to guide clinical trial management in the portfolio and the design of the portfolio, and use an illustrative numerical study motivated by pediatric oncology to show the value of using response-adaptive pilots for improving financial and health access outcomes.

detail.abstract:
This is an amicus brief in support of affirmance in EPA et al. v Green & Healthy Homes Initiative, Inc. et al., (D.C. Md. 1:25-cv-01096).  Amicus is interested in ensuring that contractors, grantees, and others who do business with the Government and/or participate in Government funded programs are treated fairly when pursuing their rights and remedies and also ensuring that public institutions (particularly the courts) appreciate and account for the many ways that Congressional mandates, public contracts, grants, cooperative agreements, and other funding mechanisms impact  the public's quality of life.

The brief asserts that the Government errs and does a disservice to the public interest in suggesting that any challenge relating to the termination of a federal grant or cooperative agreement is necessarily a garden-variety breach of contract claim that must be pigeon-holed within the cramped jurisdiction of the U.S. Court of Federal Claims.

The brief explains that: (1) federal (procurement) contracts and federal assistance agreements are distinct, fundamentally different governance tools and that different dispute resolution regimes apply to each; (2) the Court of Federal Claims' Tucker Act jurisdiction does not foreclose federal district court review of all matters related to federal assistance; and (3) that the long-familiar approach - determining the appropriate forum for each claim through the process of matter- and claim-specific consideration (Bowen, Megapulse) - makes good sense.

The brief was prepared by David Livshiz, Nathaniel Castellano, Jayna Rust, Catherine Katz & Miguel Serrano.

detail.abstract: In April 2026, the Superior Court of Quebec annulled an arbitral award for the first time in the world on the ground that the arbitrator had taken his reasoning from a generative AI tool whose every cited authority was a hallucination. The decision was reported within days across the global arbitration community. It has been read as a Quebec curiosity, as a cautionary tale for counsel, and as the empirical case that the leading skeptics of AI soft law had said did not yet exist. It is each of these things. It is also something more useful: a long-awaited application of an old principle to a new tool. The arbitrator's mandate is personal. It is the reason the parties chose this arbitrator and not another. It can be supported by tools. It cannot be transferred to them. The arbitrator may take help. The arbitrator may not transfer the decision.

detail.title: Green in the Shadow. The Information View on Green Banking Regulation

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Banking Institute Working Paper Series No. 210

detail.abstract:
We investigate the hurdles to the effective implementation of sustainable banking regulation. We argue that existing approaches rest on an implicit assumption of verifiable asset quality, which is inconsistent with the informational structure of banking. Accordingly, we develop an analytical framework centred on structural asset opacity and information asymmetry: banks operate through opaque balance sheets and possess superior information about asset quality relative to both markets and supervisors. This opacity generates moral hazard in the asset classification when regulatory incentives tied to ‘green’ or ‘brown’ labels induce strategic misrepresentation and adverse selection.

We recast the main regulatory tools proposed in the literature. The analysis shows that incorporating sustainability objectives into prudential requirements, particularly capital regulation, is prone to distortion under conditions of unverifiable information, while supervisory tools remain constrained by their reliance on bank-generated data. We advance an alternative approach based on mandatory contractual mechanisms embedded in lending relationships. Properly designed and supervised, these private law tools operate as sorting devices that differentiate between green and brown activities without requiring full information about asset quality.

detail.abstract:
The paper gives an overview on what established gatekeeper theory on financial markets was designed to achieve. It moves on to introduce three groups of AI-gatekeepers: established auditors, new entrants, and publicly accredited gatekeepers. Then, the paper describes designated AI-laws and designated AI-gatekeepers, both optional and mandatory. It concludes with a preliminary roadmap for regulating AI-gatekeepers.

The paper makes three contributions to the debate. First, it shows why a transplant of the proposal to introduce a version of strict gatekeeper liability from the financial-market setting is inadequate for AI-gatekeepers. Second, it suggests a two-layer transparency regime: aggregate disclosure of testing methodologies and standards, combined with compact certifications or scores at the individual level. Third, the paper proposes ex ante governance requirements operating at two sites: At the gatekeeper itself, through accreditation and independence requirements modelled on the EU's notified-body regime. Additionally, at the interface of the gatekeeper with the client, through institutional structures analogous to the audit committee but designed for the interdisciplinary translation problem that distinguishes AI-compliance review from classical audit.

detail.abstract: India's hydrological regime is undergoing a profound transition-from a historically predictable monsoon-driven system to a non-stationary, climate-sensitive hydrology marked by rainfall variability, altered seasonality, and the clustering of extreme events. These shifts are already reshaping reservoir management, agricultural calendars, groundwater recharge cycles, and urban drainage performance. Coupled with rapid urbanisation-projected to reach ~600 million people by 2036-intensive groundwater withdrawals and rising climate extremes are increasing systemic pressures on the country's water security. National assessments reveal multiple warning signals. CGWB (2023-24) reports persistent aquifer stress, with <10% recharge efficiency in arid basins; CPCB (2022) identifies 311 polluted river stretches, with chronic exceedances in BOD, DO, and faecal coliform levels; and MoES/INCOIS documents accelerating sea-level rise (>3 mm/yr) in the north Indian Ocean. Simultaneously, the Himalayan cryosphere is exhibiting rapid mass loss and elevated risks of Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs). This paper synthesises updated datasets from IMD, CGWB, CPCB, CWC, NRSC/ISRO, and global sources, alongside peer-reviewed literature, to map climate-water risk pathways across surface water, groundwater, urban systems, coasts, and mountain hydrology. It identifies investment-ready adaptation priorities, including Nature-based Solutions (NbS), Managed Aquifer Recharge (MAR), urban green-blue infrastructure, and IoT/AI/remote sensing-based monitoring systems. Evidence indicates that NbS can reduce peak flooding by 20-30%, increase infiltration by 15-25%, and mitigate urban heat by 2-4°C. India's pathway to climate-resilient water security demands basin-scale planning, integrated governance, circular-water transitions, and strengthened monitoring systems-supported by sustained community engagement and climate-aligned policy frameworks.

detail.abstract:
This article encourages dispute resolution practitioners to use artificial intelligence (AI) “centaur” systems, which may perform better than either humans or AI tools operating independently. Centaur systems combine human and AI capabilities so that each contributes complementary strengths in decision-making. This is particularly important in managing legal disputes, where practitioners should integrate analysis of legal issues, tangible and intangible costs, strategic judgment, and ethical considerations.

AI tools used in dispute resolution are part of an evolving ecosystem that vary in how they influence professional judgment. This includes coaching functions that help practitioners exercise judgment, advisory functions that recommend actions or strategies, and agentic functions that make decisions or take actions. As agentic functions become more prevalent, centaur systems may become particularly important in strengthening the role of professional judgment within the AI ecosystem. Because use of AI for coaching is private, low-risk, and readily available, it is an especially practical way to strengthen reflective decision-making. Repeated use of AI coaching may also help practitioners develop stronger habits of judgment that improve decision-making in contexts beyond direct AI use.

Real Practice Systems Theory helps explain how centaur systems can be implemented effectively in professional practice. This theory holds that practitioners develop unique practice systems shaped by their experience, values, habits, and recurring work demands. Practitioners can create centaur systems for themselves by selecting and using AI tools in ways that complement their own judgment. These systems can help practitioners organize complex information, identify questions that deserve closer examination, and explore alternative ways to understand disputes. Integrated into practitioners’ existing practice systems, centaur systems can promote intentional decision-making, reinforcing practitioners’ responsibility for professional judgment.

title: Upward Pricing Pressure in Linked Product and Labor Markets
affiliations: University of Florida

detail.title: Upward Pricing Pressure in Linked Product and Labor Markets
detail.abstract: Upward pricing pressure (UPP) screens for horizontal mergers usually treat product and labor markets separately. This paper derives linked-market screens in which the same merger-related adjustment affects both customers and workers. When a price change shifts business to the merger partner, it may also change that partner's employment, wages, or workers' outside options. These labor-market effects can make product-side screens too lenient or too aggressive. Likewise, product-market effects can alter labor-side screens. Thus, accounting for product-labor links can reverse whether a one-sided screen flags the merger.

title: When AI Hurts: Corporate Responsibility for Agentic AI
affiliations: York University - Osgoode Hall Law School

detail.title: When AI Hurts: Corporate Responsibility for Agentic AI
detail.abstract: As AI systems evolve from assistive tools into increasingly autonomous, agentic actors, long-standing doctrines of corporate liability are being put to the test. This Essay examines whether existing legal frameworks can hold corporations accountable for harms caused by advanced forms of AI. It suggests that, first, existing private law doctrines continue to provide a largely workable foundation without recognizing AI agency or personhood, by focusing on design, deployment, supervision, and organizational duties. Second, a doctrinal obstacle arises in systems of corporate attribution that depend on discrete human wrongs. This model becomes more fragile with agentic AI, confirming the need for depersonalized forms of corporate liability grounded in direct entity-level duties, collective wrongdoing, and organizational failures to ensure public safety. Third, even where attribution remains possible, accountability gaps persist, particularly regarding evidentiary asymmetries stemming from algorithmic opacity, difficulties in establishing causation and foreseeability, multi-actor AI ecosystems, and jurisdictional fragmentation. The Essay concludes that existing doctrines are broadly adaptable and gaps likely to be limited. Nevertheless, selective legislative measures are desirable to complement and adapt as necessary existing private law tools.

title: Are Volunteer Firefighters Adequately Protected? Evaluating Barriers to Respiratory Protection Use During Bushfire Smoke Exposure
affiliations: University of Wollongong, University of Wollongong and University of Wollongong

detail.title: Are Volunteer Firefighters Adequately Protected? Evaluating Barriers to Respiratory Protection Use During Bushfire Smoke Exposure
detail.abstract: Volunteer firefighters face recurrent exposure to hazardous airborne particles on the fireground, where toxic substances cannot be reliably predicted and often extend beyond visible flames. Despite well-established health risks, uptake of respiratory protective equipment (RPE) remains inconsistent, particularly in rural volunteer services.  This study investigated barriers to RPE use among New South Wales Rural Fire Service (NSW RFS) volunteer firefighters, examining how organisational culture, leadership, and individual factors shape respiratory protection practices.     A cross-sectional mixed-methods design was employed, consisting of an online survey (N = 613) assessing knowledge, access, training, and reported barriers to RPE use. Semi-structured interviews and focus groups with a subsample (N = 16) further explored organisational, cultural, and personal barriers. Survey data were analysed descriptively and using chi-square tests, while qualitative transcripts underwent thematic analysis.    Although 97% of respondents recognised bushfire smoke as hazardous, RPE use remained inconsistent. Common barriers included heat burden, poor fit and comfort, and communication difficulties. Organisational gaps were evident, with 76% of participants unaware of fit-testing, and inconsistent RPE issuing across brigades. Qualitative findings highlighted the influence of brigade leadership, entrenched cultural norms of toughness, operational priorities favouring speed over safety, and limited training. Firefighters exposed to compressed air breathing apparatus training reported stricter safety practices.    The findings demonstrate that awareness of respiratory hazards alone does not translate into protective behaviours. Strengthening fit-testing programs, improving individual RPE issuing, embedding respiratory protection into leadership practices, and addressing cultural perceptions of risk may help balance rapid emergency response and adherence to safety protocols.

title: The Governance Inversion Hypothesis: Why More AI Regulation May Produce Less Organisational Control

detail.title: The Governance Inversion Hypothesis: Why More AI Regulation May Produce Less Organisational Control
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Governance Inversion Hypothesis (GIH) to explain a growing paradox in artificial intelligence (AI) governance: under conditions of increasing regulatory expansion and technological complexity, organisations may become more formally governed while simultaneously experiencing a decline in operational control over AI systems. Existing AI governance frameworks generally assume that stronger regulation improves accountability, oversight, and organisational control. This paper challenges that assumption by arguing that governance formalisation itself may contribute to the erosion of control in AI-intensive environments. Drawing on institutional theory, organisational governance research, accountability scholarship, and emerging AI governance literature, the paper develops a conceptual framework explaining how regulatory expansion may weaken operational authority through four interconnected mechanisms: authority fragmentation, symbolic governance expansion, externalisation of control, and authority paralysis. As governance systems become increasingly layered and procedurally dense, organisations may struggle to maintain coherent authority, technical visibility, escalation capability, and meaningful intervention power over opaque and externally mediated AI infrastructures. The paper extends institutional decoupling theory by introducing governance inversion as a structural condition in which governance expansion may actively undermine operational coherence rather than strengthen it. It concludes that the central risk in AI governance may not be the absence of governance structures, but the emergence of institutions that appear increasingly governed while progressively losing the capacity to govern effectively.

detail.title: The Bus-Assisted Drone Delivery Problem: Integrating Public Transport and Drones for Last-Mile Delivery
detail.abstract: We consider an innovative last-mile delivery paradigm that uses drones in collaboration with public transport to deliver parcels from warehouses to customers. Drones can hitchhike on public transport during parcel delivery and/or return trips, thereby saving energy and enhancing operational efficiency. Specifically, we deliver a set of parcels from warehouses to customers using drones, in collaboration with several bus lines, aiming to minimize the sum of the completion times of all orders. This problem, referred to as the Bus-Assisted Drone Delivery Problem, is non-deterministic polynomial-time (NP)-hard. We present a compact integer programming formulation, but it can only handle small-scale instances. To address instances of meaningful size, we propose an alternative formulation with exponentially many variables. This formulation tightly couples drone routing and bus‑riding decisions. Building on this, we design a Branch-and-Price-and-Cut (BPC) algorithm with a specialized label‑setting method that uses a step‑function label representation and dominance rules to efficiently prune unpromising labels. Its speed and scalability are further strengthened by pre‑enumerating feasible labels, lower‑bounding label propagation, label‑space relaxation, and variable fixing. Extensive experiments using instances derived from real-world data are conducted. We show that the BPC algorithm significantly outperforms solving the compact formulation directly with an off-the-shelf solver (Gurobi) and highlight the substantial benefits of the proposed algorithmic enhancements. More importantly, we present valuable managerial insights. The drone service area can be significantly expanded (up to 30%) by leveraging properly selected bus lines, especially when the drone’s battery capacity is moderate. Moreover, introducing public buses can promote drone sharing among warehouses, thereby reducing the total delivery time by up to 15%. The magnitude of the reduction increases with the imbalance in warehouse demand and the number of available bus lines. Finally, we investigate the selection of bus lines and demonstrate the benefits of slightly adjusting them to align with warehouse proximity.

title: A Systematic Review of Lean Six Sigma Applications in the Semiconductor Lifecycle: From Design to E-Waste Management
affiliations: Purdue University,  and Purdue University

detail.title: A Systematic Review of Lean Six Sigma Applications in the Semiconductor Lifecycle: From Design to E-Waste Management
detail.abstract: The semiconductor industry, a cornerstone of modern technology, faces extreme challenges in sustainability, efficiency, and supply chain coordination. The application of Lean Six Sigma (LSS) methodologies offers substantial potential to address these challenges by eliminating waste, optimizing resources, and reducing variation in key processes. This paper examines the current state of LSS applications across the semiconductor lifecycle, identifies areas to improve, and proposes future research directions. Using a systematic literature review guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, we analyze relevant academic journals from the Web of Science database. Our findings highlight significant research in 10 areas, categorized into 3 groups: operational efficiency and process improvement, supply chain and collaboration, and workforce, innovation, and sustainability. While LSS methodologies have been widely adopted in semiconductor manufacturing, e-waste management, and material production, their application in other lifecycle phases-such as design, ATP (Assembly, Testing, and Packaging), and tools and equipment management-remains limited. Further research is necessary to explore the integration of LSS methodologies across all six phases of the semiconductor lifecycle, ensuring a systematic approach to industry-wide improvement.

title: The Institutional Deficit in Decentralized Autonomous Organizations - An Empirical Analysis
affiliations: University of St. Thomas - School of Law (Minnesota)

detail.title: The Institutional Deficit in Decentralized Autonomous Organizations - An Empirical Analysis
detail.abstract: This Article presents the first systematic empirical analysis of institutional architecture across decentralized autonomous organizations. Forty operational DAOs spanning eight industry segments: investment and DeFi, base-layer infrastructure, data and analytics, decentralized science, oracles and tooling, civic and political coordination, NFT collectibles, and gaming and virtual worlds. These segments are evaluated against a thirteen-category institutional rubric derived from the Calcaterra-Kaal framework. The framework synthesizes Arrow's Impossibility Theorem, the Folk Theorems of repeated games, and Incomplete Contract Theory into a proof that rule stability is institutionally self-defeating and that cooperative governance requires architecture that governs its own evolution. Five institutional patterns hold across every segment of the dataset. First, a visibility paradox: categories that produce visible artifacts (token launches, treasury balances, marketplace activity) score consistently above the midpoint, while categories that produce invisible governance infrastructure (legal wrappers, judicial branches, AI alignment policies, on-chain reputation ledgers) score consistently below it. Second, a universal AI-governance vacuum: AI Alignment scores 2.10 of 10 dataset-wide with no DAO scoring above 5, the only category in the framework where no entity crosses the midpoint. Third, token-plutocracy as the default governance form, with dataset-wide Decentralization at 5.17 and no production deployment of reputation-weighted on-chain aggregation. Fourth, legal-wrapper heterogeneity without convergence: eight distinct wrapper structures appear across the forty entities, with only one DAO using the Wyoming DAO LLC statute. Fifth, a convergent architectural agenda for institutional repair built around five upgrades: ERC-1155 multi-token reputation, tripartite separation of powers, stablecoin treasury infrastructure, weighted directed acyclic graph historiography, and values-drift detection. The unweighted dataset mean of 67.3 of 130 (51.8 percent) is the central quantitative finding: the median DAO has implemented roughly half of the institutional architecture the framework prescribes, with a projected post-upgrade mean of 95.3 representing a 42 percent improvement available through the convergent agenda. The deficit is structural rather than incidental. DAO architecture has solved the problems for which it was originally designed, decentralized capital formation and programmable value transfer, and has not yet solved the problems that emerged after its design, AI-mediated governance, Sybil-resistant identity, and constitutional separation of powers. The visibility paradox explains the under-investment: invisible institutional infrastructure is systematically underprovided relative to visible institutional infrastructure even when the invisible infrastructure is more predictive of long-run resilience. The Article develops implications for legal scholars, regulators, and DAO operators.

detail.abstract: South Africa's emerging water public-private partnership programme embeds a structural contradiction that the current policy discourse has not yet resolved: a fiscally constrained sovereign operating with a documented governance pathology at the institutional management tier has adopted the French concession model-which retains capital risk and procurement governance on the public balance sheet-rather than the English model, which transfers both to the private sector. This paper argues that the choice is not merely suboptimal. Against the diagnostic backdrop of the Auditor-General's 2024 and 2025 findings, it is analytically indefensible. The paper then demonstrates how the Adaptive Fuzzy Logic Efficiency Evaluation method (AFLEE)-developed by the author through a conceptual framework first articulated in 2005 (Eldidy, 2005) and formalised in doctoral research in 2012 (Eldidy, 2012)-provides the pre-investment screening and concession-design architecture that the English model requires to function correctly in South Africa's specific institutional context. Evidence from six utilities on four continents, assessed against 2018/2019 audited financial data, illustrates the diagnostic failures that conventional benchmarking cannot detect and that AFLEE resolves. The convergence of Ghana Water Company and Aguas Andinas at virtually identical debt-adjusted efficiency scores of approximately 31 percent-despite diametrically opposed World Bank performance ratingsis presented as the central empirical argument for a diagnostic architecture that sees financial leverage, not just operational performance.

title: Internet of Things research in Supply Chain Management and Logistics: A Bibliometric Analysis
affiliations: Széchenyi István University, Kautz Gyula Faculty of Economics, Department of Logistics and Forwarding, Students, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Higher Institute of Computer Science of El Manar, MODUL University Vienna and University of Malaya (UM)

detail.title: Internet of Things research in Supply Chain Management and Logistics: A Bibliometric Analysis
detail.abstract: This study reviews Internet of Things (IoT) research in supply chain management (SCM) and logistics. A thorough review and bibliometric analysis were conducted to analytically and objectively unearth the knowledge development in IoT research within the context of SCM and logistics. The analysis started with the selection of 807 journal articles published over a two-decade period. Then, the articles were analyzed according to bibliometric parameters such as year of publication, sources, authors, and institutions. A keyword co-occurrence network was used to cluster the pertinent literature. Results of the review and bibliometric analysis reveal that IoT research has attracted significant attention from the SCM and logistics community. Three leading journals published widely on IoT and the fifteen most productive authors are identified. Based on the keyword co-occurrence clustering, the IoT literature in SCM and logistics is focalized on RFID technology, Industry 4.0 technologies, reverse logistics, and additionally covers various industries, such as the food, retailing, construction, and the pharmaceutical sector. The study provides researchers with a better understanding of IoT research in SCM and logistics and existing knowledge gaps for further research. Practitioners may benefit from the review to keep abreast of the current discussions and applications of IoT in diverse industrial sectors. To the best of the authors' knowledge, the current review is one of the few attempts to investigate IoT research in SCM and logistics using a comprehensive set of articles published during the past two decades.

title: Navigating Geopolitical Fragmentation and Digital Transformation: A Dynamic Capabilities Perspective on Global Value Chain Resilience

detail.title: Navigating Geopolitical Fragmentation and Digital Transformation: A Dynamic Capabilities Perspective on Global Value Chain Resilience
detail.abstract: Global value chains (GVCs) are experiencing compounding disruptions driven by geopolitical fragmentation and accelerating digital transformation. Efficiency-oriented GVC strategies, optimized for stable international environments, have proven increasingly inadequate as trade protectionism, economic nationalism, and technological decoupling reshape the global business landscape. Despite the strategic significance of these converging forces, existing scholarship addresses geopolitical risk and digital transformation largely in isolation, leaving a critical theoretical gap: the absence of an integrated framework linking these dynamics to GVC resilience through organizational capabilities. This conceptual paper addresses that gap by developing an integrated theoretical framework grounded in Dynamic Capabilities Theory (Teece et al., 1997; Teece, 2020) and informed by a structured review of 87 peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025. The framework demonstrates that digital technologiesspecifically artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, and blockchainmeaningfully amplify organizational sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring capabilities. Five theoretically grounded propositions articulate the mechanisms through which digital transformation enhances GVC resilience, with dynamic capabilities serving as the mediating construct. The paper further introduces the "Glocal" strategic frameworkan integrated model combining regional hub architecture, diversified sourcing networks, and smart digital infrastructuredesigned to help firms balance operational efficiency with systemic resilience. These contributions offer actionable guidance for executives, supply chain managers, and policymakers navigating the complex trade-offs of contemporary global operations.

detail.abstract: Compartmental models have been a phenomenon of studying epidemics. However, existing compartmental models do not explicitly consider the spatial spread of an epidemic and logistics issues simultaneously. In this study, we address this limitation by introducing a new epidemicslogistics mixed-integer programming (MIP) model that determines the optimal amount, timing and location of resources that are allocated for controlling an infectious disease outbreak while accounting for its spatial spread dynamics. The objective of this proposed model is to minimize the total number of infections and fatalities under a limited budget over a multi-period planning horizon. The present study is the first spatially explicit optimization approach that considers geographically varying rates for disease transmission, migration of infected individuals over different regions, and varying treatment rates due to the limited capacity of treatment centers. We illustrate the performance of the MIP model using the case of the 2014-2015 Ebola outbreak in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. Our results provide explicit information on intervention timing and intensity for each specific region of these most affected countries. title: Moat Half-Life: Modeling Competitive Advantage in Technology Companies

detail.title: Moat Half-Life: Modeling Competitive Advantage in Technology Companies
detail.abstract: Traditional competitive moat analysis treats defensive advantages as binary-present or absent and implicitly static. This paper introduces a quantitative framework, Moat Half-Life, that models competitive advantages as dynamic assets subject to exponential decay. The framework defines moat half-life as the estimated period over which a competitive advantage loses half its defensive strength, measured through a decay function governed by three structural parameters: CapEx Velocity (the rate at which competitors can deploy capital to replicate the advantage), Open-Source Parity (the speed at which open-source alternatives commoditize proprietary capabilities), and Distribution Friction (the switching costs and behavioral inertia that slow user migration). The framework is applied to three technology companies-Alphabet (GOOGL), NVIDIA (NVDA), and Amazon (AMZN)-across twenty-one distinct competitive moat layers, producing asset-by-asset half-life estimates ranging from three years (software runtime ecosystems) to eleven years (EUV lithography monopoly). A formalized Moat Strength Score (MSS) decay function, MSS(t) = 100 × (0.5) t/h, enables portfolio-level resilience modeling with milestone-driven recalibration. The paper demonstrates that moat half-lives in technology markets are compressing due to accelerating AI capability deployment, but that self-reinforcing platform network effects and physical infrastructure moats exhibit meaningfully longer durability than manufacturing or software stack advantages. Case study evidence from Google I/O 2026 product announcements illustrates how specific corporate actions extend or erode individual moat half-lives in real time.

title: Private Interest in the Public Good: Cholera and the Origins of Sanitary Reform
affiliations: University of Wageningen and

detail.title: Private Interest in the Public Good: Cholera and the Origins of Sanitary Reform
detail.abstract: European countries paved the way for modern economic growth in the 19th century with large-scale reforms facilitating human capital accumulation. The literature has looked at the role of elites in broad education investments, but less attention has been devoted to reforms promoting workers' health, a key component of human capital. This paper studies the impact of the 1866 cholera outbreak on modern waterworks construction in the German Empire to test the hypothesis whether concerns about workers' health may have compelled elites to invest in health-enhancing public goods. We find that the epidemic raised the annual probability of building waterworks by about 35%. Exogenous variation relying on the cholera-spreading effect of military movements during the Austro-Prussian War in 1866 further underpins this result. Quantitative and qualitative evidence indicates that non-agricultural elites employing more productive capital and better-skilled workers pushed for reform to avoid the costly prospect of future labour shocks. Long-term analyses show sizeable and persisting effects of the epidemic on public health and development outcomes shortly before the First World War.

title: The Price of Protection: Tariff Incidence and Import Collapse Under the Infamous Smoot-Hawley Tariff
affiliations: Santa Clara University - Leavey School of Business - Economics Department and Inter-American Development Bank

detail.title: The Price of Protection: Tariff Incidence and Import Collapse Under the Infamous Smoot-Hawley Tariff
detail.abstract: Using newly digitized monthly data on the quantities and prices of imports as well as product-level data on tariff rates, we estimate that in the first year after the passage of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, imports facing rate increases fell swiftly and dramatically relative to imports not affected by tariffs: for a one-percentage-point increase in the tariff rate, they declined by an average of 4%. We also estimate that the incidence of Smoot-Hawley was almost entirely borne by U.S. importers. Using an open-economy model, we attribute our high measured short-run trade elasticity of greater than 4 to fixed exchange rates that the U.S. maintained with most trade partners in the first 15 months after enactment. Our model also suggests that Smoot-Hawley accounted for 27% of the decline in total US imports in the first year after enactment. Finally, we construct both partial equilibrium and general equilibrium welfare estimates of Smoot-Hawley. Both methods deliver welfare losses of about 0.2% of GDP, reflecting the high measured elasticity of substitution and low US import-GDP ratio.

title: On Causal Inference with Model-Based Outcomes
affiliations: Centre for Monetary and Financial Studies (CEMFI), Centre for Monetary and Financial Studies (CEMFI) and Centre for Monetary and Financial Studies (CEMFI)

detail.title: On Causal Inference with Model-Based Outcomes
detail.abstract: We study the estimation of causal effects on group-level parameters identified from microdata (e.g., child penalties). We demonstrate that standard one-step methods (such as pooled OLS and IV regressions) are generally inconsistent due to an endogenous weighting bias, where the policy affects the implicit weights (e.g., altering fertility rates). In contrast, we advocate for a two-step Minimum Distance (MD) framework that explicitly separates parameter identification from policy evaluation. This approach eliminates the endogenous weighting bias and requires explicitly confronting sample selection when groups are small, thereby improving transparency. We show the MD estimator performs well when parameters can be estimated for most groups, and propose a robust alternative that uses auxiliary information in settings with limited data. To illustrate the importance of this methodological choice, we evaluate the effect of the 2005 Dutch childcare reform on child penalties and find that the conventional one-step approach yields estimates that are substantially larger than those from the two-step method.

title: Cues, Attention, and Charitable Giving
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam,  and Frankfurt School of Finance & Management

detail.title: Cues, Attention, and Charitable Giving
detail.abstract: We identify cue-based beliefs as a source of context dependence in charitable giving. Adapting associative memory models to donations, we predict that cues shift giving by changing which beneficiaries and needs come to mind, even when the cues are uninformative about the donation decision. In online experiments, cues that draw attention to global needs increase giving to an international cause, whereas cues that draw attention to local needs reduce it. Open-ended text responses confirm the attentional mechanism. Applying the framework to fundraising design, we predict that neighborhood-based group appeals–which can raise giving when the charity's mission is local–may backfire when the charity's mission is global. In a natural field experiment with 105,000 donors to a charity with a global mission, such an appeal reduces pledge take-up by 33%. A complementary online experiment replicates this effect and shows that the appeal shifts attention toward local recipients and away from global ones. Heterogeneity reinforces this interpretation because, in both settings, the group appeal backfires most where baseline behavior suggests that global needs would otherwise have been more likely to come to mind. The results help organize evidence on media-driven shifts in giving, boomerang effects of norm nudges, failures of priming interventions to replicate, and the sensitivity of redistribution preferences to salient recipients.

title: Separations Revisited: Do Layoffs or Quits Drive Lower Separation Rates in High-Quality Firms?
affiliations: Georgetown University, CEMFI and Centre for Monetary and Financial Studies (CEMFI)

detail.title: Separations Revisited: Do Layoffs or Quits Drive Lower Separation Rates in High-Quality Firms?
detail.abstract: We challenge the view that the negative correlation between firm quality and separation rates reflects efficient separations. Using Brazilian administrative data, we show that this correlation is driven by lower layoff rates at high-quality firms, not differences in quits. We develop a job search model where wage rigidity and productivity uncertainty generate inefficient layoffs. The model predicts that higher-quality firms have larger markdowns and, consequently, fewer layoffs. Empirically, we validate this by showing that firms facing stronger wage rigidity have higher layoffs and a steeper quality-layoff correlation, and that markdowns are higher in better firms and negatively correlated with layoffs.
